card.hook: Down on the sand, Patong is a blur of umbrellas and elbows. From up high, the whole 2.85 km (1.77 miles) curve of the bay fits in one frame, and that's the shot to go for.
card.stand_here: Stand at Patong Beach Viewpoint on Thawewong Road, the hillside road above the beach, and face the bay with the beach laid out below you. From there Patong Beach is about 960 m to the south (roughly 15 minutes on foot), so check the exact spot on the map.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to catch the whole curve of the bay, then go to 1x for a more natural view. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out umbrellas, boats or people on the sand.
card.make_it_pop: Around sunset, tap the brightest part of the sky, then slide it a bit darker so the sunset colours don't wash out.
card.best_time: Aim for sunset, when the light turns warm and the lights start to come on along the front. Get there a little early to grab a good spot.
card.selfie_here: Try the open top-floor terrace of Samutr Bar at Amari Phuket, at the southern end of Patong Beach. Stand by the row of pale stools with the pool below, use the front camera at 0.5x, and let the bay sweep out behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: At the rocky headland at the north end of Patong, near Kalim Beach, stand on the rocks with the whole Patong crescent behind you and ask a passer-by to shoot from in front of you, ideally around golden hour.
card.rules_and_safety: The viewpoint is listed as free, but check local signs before you go. If you head down to the beach, Patong often has high waves in the low season and a red flag is raised there most often, so never ignore it.
card.challenge: Pop your gridlines on, put the line where sand meets sea on the lower third, keep the horizon dead level, and see if you can spot the smallest boat in the bay.
card.good_to_know: Patong is the busiest beach resort on Phuket's west coast and became popular with Western visitors in the late 1980s. Today it's the island's main tourist resort, with lots of hotels and the heart of its shopping and nightlife. The town was hit hard by the tsunami of 26 December 2004, but it has largely recovered.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Patong Beach Viewpoint on Thawewong Road, the hillside road above the beach, and face the bay with the beach laid out below you. From there Patong Beach is about 960 m to the south (roughly 15 minutes on foot), so check the exact spot on the map.

card.hook: Look up! In Phuket Old Town the best bits are often on the upper floors, above the café tables and shop signs, and most people walk right past them.
card.stand_here: Stand near ถนนถลาง, about 370 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Take your main photos on the pavement at a street corner.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x for whole street scenes, then go to 1x for shopfronts. Try 2x to 5x for upper-floor details and signs (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the shophouse verticals straight, then tap the brightest wall and nudge it a little darker so the colours don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning or late in the afternoon. The streets are likely to be quieter and the light softer.
card.selfie_here: Stand in the middle of Soi Romanee with the pastel shophouse fronts on both sides behind you, using the front camera at 0.5x. The pink and mint walls look great in soft morning light. You can also try one corner of the Chartered Bank crossing with the old bank building behind you, but check the corner on the map first.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the opposite corner across the crosswalk, facing you, while you stand on the bank corner, so they can fit the bank and the whole intersection into one wide shot.
card.rules_and_safety: The streets are open public space, but individual museums, shops and restaurants have their own rules, so check the official site before you go in. Keep an eye on traffic when you step back to compose.
card.challenge: Find a doorway, sign or café table to use as your foreground, then shoot one street with a repeating row of shopfronts leading your eye to the far corner.
card.good_to_know: The area grew rich on tin mining, and Hokkien Chinese miners did much of the work in the 18th century. In the early 20th century, roads and canals were built and European mining companies were invited in. Many buildings from that time have been preserved and restored, and the area is also tied to the Baba community.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near ถนนถลาง, about 370 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Take your main photos on the pavement at a street corner.

card.hook: Down on Kata Beach you get sunbeds, restaurants and a lot of elbows. Climb the hill road south and the whole bay goes calm, turquoise and a bit smug about it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Kata Noi Viewpoint, the small roadside lookout on the road between Kata and Nai Harn, and face the bay below. The beach position on the map is about 1.5 km to the north of the viewpoint.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the curve of the bay and the sky, then switch to 1x for a tidier crop of water and sand. If your phone has 2x to 5x, use it to look for the Big Buddha on the far hill on a clear day.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the top or bottom third line, and keep it level.
card.best_time: Go at sunset, when the cove is at its most atmospheric. Arrive a little early to grab a spot at the roadside.
card.selfie_here: For a classic selfie, try the main viewing platform at Karon Viewpoint (Three Beaches Hill). Use the front camera at 0.5x with the three-bay panorama behind you over your shoulder. For a colourful backdrop, the South Beach Mural on the southern part of Kata Beach, between Beyond Kata and The Boathouse Phuket, could work with the sand and sea in the frame.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the sidewalk just above the sand near the northern beach entrance (the umbrella zone) while you stand on the beach, so the sea and Koh Pu sit behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: At the roadside, stay off the carriageway and watch for passing scooters. The roadside view is free, but the best terrace spots belong to the café and are for customers. Visit in daylight for safety and better photos.
card.challenge: Can you spot the Big Buddha on the distant hill? Zoom in, snap it, and call it a Where's Wally win.
card.good_to_know: Kata Beach is a 1.5-kilometre stretch of sand facing the Andaman Sea, split into Kata Yai in the north and Kata Noi in the south. Access to the Big Buddha has been closed since a landslide in August 2024, so this distant glimpse may be the nearest you get. For all three bays in one wide frame, with little Koh Pu just off Kata, the Karon Viewpoint is the alternative, though it gets very crowded at sunset.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Kata Noi Viewpoint, the small roadside lookout on the road between Kata and Nai Harn, and face the bay below. The beach position on the map is about 1.5 km to the north of the viewpoint.

card.hook: Karon Beach is so long you can finally step back and fit the whole sweep of sand into one shot. Add paddlers at the water's edge, a couple strolling and kids splashing in the shallows, and the scene is ready for you.
card.stand_here: Head up to Karon Viewpoint, the hilltop platform, and face north over the bays. It's on a hill rather than on the sand, so check the map pin before you set off.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the full sweep of sand and sea. Switch to 1x for natural-looking scenes with people, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for details far away.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon or the waterline on a line so your shot looks nice and level.
card.best_time: Late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on this west-facing coast. Early morning is often calmer, and midday sun is harsh and flattens the colours.
card.selfie_here: Stand on the main platform at Karon Viewpoint, right by the 'Karon Viewpoint' sign, with the curve of the road and the three bays behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a bit low so the bays fit over your shoulder. Another option is the wooden sign on the deck railing at On The Hill Karon (the viewpoint restaurant on the hill road above Karon), which puts the whole curve of the beach behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand near the 'Karon Viewpoint' sign and the curve of the road, with you in front of them and Kata Noi, Kata and Karon beaches in the background.
card.rules_and_safety: Mind the edge and respect other visitors' space when shooting.
card.challenge: Pick a gap in your frame and wait for a walker to stroll into it, no chasing allowed. Patience pays off.
card.good_to_know: Karon is the second longest beach in Phuket province, and it's generally quieter than neighbouring Patong. It has a loyal Scandinavian following, and many local businesses cater to them. The 2004 tsunamis badly damaged the beach, especially in the south, but it had largely recovered by 2008.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head up to Karon Viewpoint, the hilltop platform, and face north over the bays. It's on a hill rather than on the sand, so check the map pin before you set off.

card.hook: Here's the funny thing about a giant seated Buddha: he's far too big for your phone's default view, so you'll be stepping backwards like you're dodging a puddle. The open space around him makes him a lovely, simple subject once you do.
card.stand_here: Stand about 30 m south-west of the statue, at the phone icon on the map near ซอยยอดเสน่ห์ 1, and face north-east. If he still won't fit, take a few steps back rather than tilting your phone up.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole statue in with plenty of sky above his head, and keep your phone level so the sides don't lean in. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for a calm, close shot of the face or folded hands.
card.make_it_pop: A bright sky can wash the statue out, so tap the statue and slide the brightness down a little, and switch on the gridlines to keep his base straight.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and a bluer sky. Midday sun can be harsh and wash out the detail.
card.selfie_here: Try the south railing of the main terrace, facing the coastline: switch to the front camera, use zoom 0.5x and the statue should end up behind your shoulder. The platform on the statue's left side, looking out over Kata Beach, is another good option.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by at the lower car park area to shoot wide, as from there they can fit the whole statue in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Please take photos quietly and respectfully, and check local signs for any visiting rules. Drones are prohibited unless you have written permission. Reports differ on whether access is open right now, so check locally before you set off.
card.challenge: Take one photo with a few visitors in the frame, so everyone can see just how big he really is.
card.good_to_know: The Big Buddha is a large seated Buddha statue on Phuket island. It ranks 5th among the photo spots on our Phuket map. Visitors may walk through your frame, so wait a moment for a clearer view.

card.hook: The first thing you'll notice at Wat Chalong is the roof: layer after layer of red and gold, with fancy tassels and serpent decorations, all set against the sky. It's loud in the best way, and it makes your photo look good without much effort.
card.stand_here: Stand at Wat Chalong, outside the ordination hall (the ubosot), where you can frame its roofline against the sky. Face west, towards the middle of the temple grounds.
card.zoom: Use 1x to get the whole ordination hall in. Go to 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the roof tassels and serpent decorations. Try 0.5x only if you're close and want the full height of the roof.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the roof edges straight, then tap the bright sky or the gold trim and slide a little darker so the sky stays blue and the red and gold stay rich.
card.best_time: Go early, before the tour coaches roll in from mid-morning. You'll get fewer people in your frame and softer light.
card.selfie_here: Head to the gardens around the temple grounds and put the temple buildings behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit more in, and keep the temple over your shoulder. Guides call it a calm green backdrop, but they don't name an exact spot, so wander until the view looks right.
card.ask_someone: Stand in the garden in front of the main chedi (the Grand Pagoda) and ask your photographer to stand back facing you, so the pagoda fills the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: This is a working temple, so dress respectfully and keep the flash off. Ask before photographing monks or worshippers, skip photos during ceremonies and prayer times, and watch for no-photo signs in inner rooms. Photography of the relic chamber inside the Grand Pagoda is restricted.
card.challenge: Find a serpent decoration on the roof, zoom in to 2x or more, and get it sharp with a tassel beside it.
card.good_to_know: Wat Chalong is the most important of Phuket's 29 Buddhist temples, and its official name is Wat Chaiyathararam. It honours two respected monks, Luang Pho Chaem and Luang Pho Chuang. In 1876 they led the people of Chalong against the Chinese rebellion and used their herbal medicine knowledge to help the injured.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Wat Chalong, outside the ordination hall (the ubosot), where you can frame its roofline against the sky. Face west, towards the middle of the temple grounds.

card.hook: Picture a cliff-edge platform at sunset, packed with people all holding their phones up at the same sky. That's Promthep Cape in peak season, and the car park can be full by about 17:30.
card.stand_here: Head to the cliff-edge main platform at Promthep Cape and face west toward the Andaman Sea. You'll have the rocky point and its palm-lined edge in front of you, with islands out on the horizon.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the headland, palms and sea in one go. If the platform is busy, drop to 0.5x for the whole sweep of coast and sky, or try 2x to 5x (depends on your phone) to pick out the islands or bring the lighthouse closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the top or bottom line, then tap the brightest part of the sky and slide it a little darker so the sunset colours don't wash out.
card.best_time: Go around sunset, and check the sunset time for your date because it changes through the year. In peak season, aim to arrive 45 to 90 minutes early so you get a parking space and a good spot on the platform.
card.selfie_here: Walk down the dirt trail from the upper platform toward the lighthouse to the lower viewpoint. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the rocks and sea fill the frame behind you. Most people stay at the upper railing, so you'll likely have fewer people in your shot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the small roadside pull-off between Ya Nui Beach and the cape car park and face back toward the cape and lighthouse, while you pose with them in the background.
card.rules_and_safety: The path down to the lower viewpoint is steep, so take it slowly. Stay off the rocks near the waterline: the waves there can be unpredictable and powerful, visitors have been swept into the sea, and there are no lifeguards in that area.
card.challenge: Take the same sunset three times, once when the sky is pale, once when it warms up and once at the glow, then pick your winner.
card.good_to_know: Promthep Cape (Laem Phromthep in Thai) is a rocky headland on Phuket, close to Ya Nui Beach, where the land meets the Andaman Sea. The white Kanchanaphisek Lighthouse looks great against the evening sky and you can photograph it from outside, but entry is restricted, so check locally. The Windmill Viewpoint shows Ya Nui Beach with the cape far off across the bay, so the cape looks small from there.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the cliff-edge main platform at Promthep Cape and face west toward the Andaman Sea. You'll have the rocky point and its palm-lined edge in front of you, with islands out on the horizon.

card.hook: Most theme parks wait for sunshine. Phuket FantaSea waits for dark, then lights up a Sukhothai-style stone elephant palace so it glows gold.
card.stand_here: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, inside the Phuket FantaSea grounds. There's no further walking, because the icon sits at the subject itself. Face the big temple-style buildings and lit-up surroundings, and if it's busy, shuffle a few steps sideways for a clear line.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit a whole building in. Use 1x for most shots, then 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out carvings and roof details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the building's straight lines upright, then tap a bright part of the building and slide it a little darker so the lights don't blow out.
card.best_time: Come in the evening, because this is a nighttime park. Dusk is the sweet spot, when the sky still has some colour and the lights are already on.
card.selfie_here: Try the main entrance gate (the Elephant Palace gate) in the early evening, before the show, with the gate behind you. The night lighting on the gold architecture makes a strong backdrop. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold the phone a bit low so the gate stays over your shoulder. For a second shot, stand beside the giant sculpture outside the theatre with the theatre building behind you, which makes the building look even bigger.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos and video aren't allowed inside the theatre during the main show, and phones must go in lockers before you enter. The show's explosive effects and loud sounds may be intense for young children. Check the official site before you go and follow staff instructions on the day.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of a whole building, then hunt down a single carving and make it the star of a close-up.
card.good_to_know: Phuket FantaSea opened on 20 December 1998 and covers about 60 acres (20 ha). The show is staged in the Palace of the Elephants, a three-floor theatre that seats 3,000. Next door, the Golden Kinnaree buffet is built in an Ayutthaya-era style and seats 4,000 guests.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand right at the phone icon on the map, inside the Phuket FantaSea grounds. There's no further walking, because the icon sits at the subject itself. Face the big temple-style buildings and lit-up surroundings, and if it's busy, shuffle a few steps sideways for a clear line.

card.hook: Most people snap Nai Harn with their toes in the sand, but the real show is from above. Up on the hill, the whole bay curves out below you, and a few white wind turbines wander into the frame like they planned it.
card.stand_here: Stand on Windmill Viewpoint, the hilltop between Nai Harn and Ya Nui beaches. Face north: Nai Harn Bay and its crescent of sand lie below you, with Ya Nui Beach and Promthep Cape in the distance.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole bay and the turbines in one shot. Switch to 1x for a tidier, more natural look, then try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out Promthep Cape or Ya Nui Beach.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and set the curve of the beach along the lower third line, so sea and sky fill the rest.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to sunset is the usual favourite. If you want the clearest, stillest water, try early morning instead, and remember the monsoon season runs from May to October.
card.selfie_here: Try Nai Harn Viewpoint Hill, a short climb up from the sand behind the beach, and go after 3 PM for less glare. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x and turn so the bay sits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the lake side, on the shore of Nai Harn Lake behind the beach, facing the sea, while you stand on the sand with the beach behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Windmill Viewpoint is described as a free, open hilltop, but check locally before you go. If you fancy Black Rock Viewpoint too, its access road is described as hard to find, so check the route first.
card.challenge: Get a turbine at one edge and the beach curve on the lower third line, then see if a friend can spot which one is the 'character' of the shot.
card.good_to_know: Nai Harn Beach is a crescent of sand on Phuket's Andaman coast. It's quieter than Promthep Cape and, as far as we know, free to visit. Down on the sand, granite boulders make a good foreground with the green hill behind.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Windmill Viewpoint, the hilltop between Nai Harn and Ya Nui beaches. Face north: Nai Harn Bay and its crescent of sand lie below you, with Ya Nui Beach and Promthep Cape in the distance.

card.hook: Picture a cluster of tall white wind turbines on a little hilltop, with the Andaman Sea dropping away on the other side. It's a lot of drama for a spot that's right off the road.
card.stand_here: Stand on the hilltop where the phone icon sits on the map, then walk to the edge of the flat, wide top, away from the turbines. Face south and you'll see open sea and Promthep Cape with its access path.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x for the big sweep of sea and headland, or for the turbines with sky above. Switch to 1x for a cleaner, less stretched view of the cape, and try 2x to 5x if your phone has it to pull the headland closer.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the upper or lower third line, and keep the headland off-centre.
card.best_time: Late afternoon into sunset has the most atmosphere, but the small car park fills up then, so get there early. Earlier in the day it's quieter and easier to find space on the top.
card.selfie_here: Try the western side of the covered sala (the shaded pavilion) at the top, ideally before 6 PM for sunset light. Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x, and hold the phone a bit low so the turbines and sea fit in behind your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from a little further back on the ridge near the sala, not at the cliff edge, so both the turbines and Promthep Cape fit in with you in front.
card.rules_and_safety: There's no railing or barrier at the edge, so watch your footing near the slope, especially with children. Keep back from the edge when you compose, and take care holding your phone out over the view in wind.
card.challenge: Get two shots from one hilltop: one with a single tall turbine towering in the foreground, and one with no turbines at all, just sea, headland and a straight horizon.
card.good_to_know: Windmill Viewpoint is a small hilltop on Wisit Road, between Nai Harn and Ya Nui beaches in the far south of Phuket. The turbines are part of the Promthep Alternative Energy Station. It's a free, open public hilltop, but the road up is steep and winding and tuk-tuks can slow traffic, so allow a little extra time and check locally before you go.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the hilltop where the phone icon sits on the map, then walk to the edge of the flat, wide top, away from the turbines. Face south and you'll see open sea and Promthep Cape with its access path.

card.hook: The first locals you meet on Khao Rang might be monkeys in the car park, but the real star is the view from the top. Phuket Town's old-town grid of streets and rooftops is laid out below you like a map.
card.stand_here: Head up to the summit terrace and stand right at the phone icon on the map, which marks the spot. Face out over the town and the coast, with the white domed pavilion in the corner of your frame.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the town with the pavilion in the corner. Go to 0.5x when you want the whole dome, garden and sky in one shot. Try zoom 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out bits of the old-town grid and the coastline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the pavilion on one side, and at sunset tap the town and drag the slider to make it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Sunset and city-light time, 17:00-18:30, is the showpiece, but it can get busy. For a calmer visit, go 07:00-09:00. After dark, use night mode and rest your phone on a wall or railing to keep it steady.
card.selfie_here: Try the balcony that juts out in front of the hilltop tower. It gives you a wide, roughly 180-degree Phuket Town backdrop and is usually not crowded. Use the front camera (0.5x if yours has it) and let the view sit behind your shoulder. The corners of the Phraya Ratsadanupradit Hall of Fame building also make a striking backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Down the hill from the top terrace, the lower panoramic platform next to Tunk-Ka Café is a good place to ask a passer-by for a photo; stand with the view behind you and check the framing on the spot, as we haven't confirmed whether the whole landmark fits.
card.rules_and_safety: Monkeys roam the car park and grounds, so keep a safe distance, keep food out of sight and don't hold your phone loosely near them. The white pavilion has reportedly been partly covered during renovations, so check its current state before you go.
card.challenge: Get one photo with the pavilion in the corner, a level horizon, and a bit of terrace edge in the foreground, with no monkey in sight.
card.good_to_know: Khao Rang is the hill above Phuket Town. It isn't high, but the summit still shows the old-town grid. The summit is free to enter and open all day, with a terrace, a landscaped garden and the white domed pavilion.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head up to the summit terrace and stand right at the phone icon on the map, which marks the spot. Face out over the town and the coast, with the white domed pavilion in the corner of your frame.

card.hook: Picture a tidy, colourful 1934 mansion tucked on a quiet side street, with an arched doorway that practically asks you to centre it. That's the Phuket Thai Hua Museum, and you can get the shot before you even think about buying a ticket.
card.stand_here: Stand on Krabi Road, on the street right in front of the Phuket Thai Hua Museum, where the phone icon sits. Face the front facade and step back until you can fit the whole thing in.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole front. If the street's too narrow to fit both storeys, switch to 0.5x. Then try 2x or more to home in on the plasterwork and shutters.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, centre the arch, and keep the phone level so the walls and shutters stay straight.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon is what one guide suggests for exterior photos, so aim for those.
card.selfie_here: Use the front courtyard at 28 Krabi Road and turn so the museum's facade is right behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and try 0.5x if your phone offers it, so the arched entrance fits over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos of the exterior and courtyard are free. Photos inside need an extra 200 baht photo pass on top of the 200 baht entry, with no flash. Please don't touch the displays.
card.challenge: Take a straight-on shot of the whole front, then a close-up of the plasterwork around a window. Bonus points if your shutters come out dead straight.
card.good_to_know: The museum sits in a 1934 mansion in Phuket Old Town, on Krabi Road just east of Thalang Road. The facade is Sino-Portuguese, with an arched entrance, shuttered windows and decorative plasterwork. For a quieter second shot, look for the older-looking corner at the back, where old roof tiles are stacked. If you want to shoot inside, check opening days before you go.

card.hook: Down on the sand, Kamala feels like any other lovely beach. Go a little way off and the whole long curve shows up at once, with the Andaman Sea behind it.
card.stand_here: Stand at Laem Singh Viewpoint, the roadside lookout on the headland between Kamala and Surin, about 860 m north-west of the beach. Face south-east, looking back over Kamala, and you'll see the beach curving below a palm-fringed headland.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole bay in. Then try 1x for a calmer, more natural look, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the headland or one stretch of sand.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, run the sweep of the beach along a diagonal, and let a few palm leaves poke in at one edge to frame it.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is the favourite here for sunset shots. Trees can block the sun from the lookout, so look at the sky and the trees before you settle in, and leave time to try another spot if they do.
card.selfie_here: Head to the north end of Kamala Beach, on the smooth sand near the palms, and turn your back to the sea. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x, and hold the phone a little low so the palms and beach both fit over your shoulder. For a more local feel, the southern end has parked long-tail boats you can pop in behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at Kamala Beach View Point (next to Novotel Resort, past Café del Mar) while you wave from the beach below, so the whole bay fits in behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Laem Singh lookout is a roadside stop with no entry fee. If you visit Wat Baan Kamala, check the official site first and dress respectfully.
card.challenge: Get the sand curving corner to corner through your picture, with one palm leaf in the frame and not a single thumb.
card.good_to_know: Kamala Beach is a long curve of sand on Phuket's west side, facing the open Andaman Sea. The Laem Singh lookout sits on the headland between Kamala and Surin. If you're at the north end of the beach, you can walk there along the coastal road.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at Laem Singh Viewpoint, the roadside lookout on the headland between Kamala and Surin, about 860 m north-west of the beach. Face south-east, looking back over Kamala, and you'll see the beach curving below a palm-fringed headland.
